# CatalystCalendarData

Source: https://www.tradingview.com/script/JaxGqEl9-CatalystCalendarData/

## Description

Data component of the Catalyst economic calendar indicator.

WHAT THIS CONTAINS

A compiled release schedule for economic and commodity events across US, Euro
Area, UK, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Switzerland and China, plus
energy and agricultural reports, Treasury auctions and market-structure dates.

Roughly 24 months of history and 12 months of forward schedule.

The schedule is compiled offline from official agency calendars: the Federal
Reserve, FRED, the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the US Energy Information
Administration, and the published policy meeting calendars of the ECB, Bank of
England, Bank of Canada, Reserve Bank of Australia, Reserve Bank of New Zealand,
Bank of Japan and Swiss National Bank.

This library holds dates only. Released values are read separately through
request.economic().

EXPORTS

monthChunk(year, month)  the encoded occurrence records for one UTC month
keyTable()               event metadata, one record per line
buildStamp()             UTC milliseconds at which this data was generated
horizon()                the first and last timestamp covered

FORMAT

Each occurrence is a fixed-width 10-character record, DDHHMMKKKI. The encoding is
documented inline in the source in enough detail to decode a record by hand.

UPDATE CADENCE

Regenerated and republished quarterly. Scripts pin a version number, so an
existing import keeps working until it is deliberately updated.
```

---

## Source Code

````pine
// This source code is subject to the terms of the Mozilla Public License 2.0 at https://mozilla.org/MPL/2.0/
// © Gigi_Luigino
//
// ===========================================================================
// Catalyst Calendar Data
// ===========================================================================
//
// The embedded release schedule for "Catalyst: Multi-Asset Economic Calendar".
// This library holds DATA ONLY. It reads nothing, requests nothing and draws
// nothing: four functions that return the schedule the indicator decodes.
//
// WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE PUBLICATION
//
//   The calendar was one file by design, and stayed that way through six
//   batches. It stopped being possible: a script's own compiled form is capped
//   at roughly 100,000 tokens, and the schedule alone compiles to more than
//   that once every event carries a plain-English description.
//
//   An imported library draws from a SEPARATE budget of up to 1,000,000
//   tokens. Splitting does not make the data smaller - it puts it somewhere
//   with room for it.
//
// WHAT IT EXPORTS
//
//   monthChunk(y, m)  packed occurrence records for one UTC month, or ""
//   keyTable()        event metadata, one newline-separated row per event
//   buildStamp()      UTC milliseconds at which this data was generated
//   horizon()         [start, end] of the generated range, UTC milliseconds
//
// THE FORMAT IS DOCUMENTED IN FULL BELOW, and deliberately so. The data is
// plain text, not compressed and not obfuscated, and the comment block under
// this one is enough to decode any record by hand with a text editor. Open
// source that nobody can verify is worse than closed source.
//
// GENERATED. Do not edit this file - edit the pipeline's taxonomy and run
// `gigi build`, or the next build discards your changes.
//
// ===========================================================================

//@version=6
library("CatalystCalendarData", overlay = false)

//#region [Data]
// ===================================================================
// GENERATED FILE - DO NOT EDIT BY HAND.
//
// Produced by the CATALYST pipeline (`gigi build`). Edit the taxonomy
// or codegen.py and regenerate; hand edits are lost on the next build.
//
// Built    : 2026-09-14 08:37 UTC
// Horizon  : 2024-09 to 2027-09  (37 monthly chunks)
// Events   : 118 canonical, 5614 occurrences
//
// -------------------------------------------------------------------
// HOW TO DECODE THIS BY HAND
// -------------------------------------------------------------------
//
// Two structures: a key table of metadata, and one chunk of packed
// occurrence records per calendar month. Nothing is compressed or
// obfuscated - you can verify any row with a text editor.
//
// THIS REGION LIVES IN A LIBRARY, and the four functions below are
// exported. It is not a preference: an indicator's own compiled form
// is capped at roughly 100,000 tokens and this data alone exceeds it,
// while an imported library draws from a separate budget of up to
// 1,000,000. Moving the data does not shrink it - it moves it
// somewhere with room. See ARCHITECTURE section 1.
//
// monthChunks() and CHUNK_BASE_YM are deliberately NOT
// exported. They are how the chunks are stored, not what a caller
// needs, and an exported name is a promise to keep it working.
//
// KEY TABLE - one line per event, '|' delimited:
//
//     KKK|NAME|RGN|CAT|TVF|UNIT|DEC|POL|SCL|DRV|DESC
//
//     KKK   base36 index, matches the occurrence record
//     NAME  display name
//     RGN   US EU GB JP AU NZ CA CH CN XX   (XX = global)
//     CAT   POL INF LAB GRO HOU SEN ENE MET AGR POS AUC MKT
//     TVF   request.economic() field code, empty if no series exists
//     UNIT  display suffix: % K M B T Bcf kbbl idx or empty
//     DEC   decimals to render, 0-3
//     POL   1 = a higher print is bullish for the currency,
//          -1 = inverted (unemployment, jobless claims),
//           0 = neutral. This is what makes the Change column's
//           colouring correct: a falling unemployment rate is a
//           smaller number and better news, and POL is what says so.
//     SCL   divisor applied to the RAW series value before display.
//           request.economic() returns unscaled units: payrolls arrive
//           as 57000, not 57. SCL is 1000 there, 1000000 for barrels,
//           1 for percentages and index levels.
//     DRV   0 = the field already returns the number we display.
//           1 = display month-on-month % change, computed here.
//           2 = display year-on-year % change, computed here.
//
//           DRV is non-zero only where the data provider publishes an
//           index LEVEL and no rate variant of it. Core PCE is the
//           case that forced this: it is the Fed's preferred inflation
//           gauge, and the only field available returns 130.27 - a
//           correct, useless number, since nobody trades the level.
//
//           The rate is computed from the series' own history. Values
//           are back-dated to the end of their reference period, so
//           sampling at each release gives exactly one sample per
//           period, and:
//
//               mom = (sample[0] / sample[1]  - 1) * 100
//               yoy = (sample[0] / sample[12] - 1) * 100
//
//           Until that many samples exist the cell is blank rather
//           than wrong. UNIT and DEC describe the DERIVED value, so a
//           DRV row reads '%' even though its field is an index; SCL
//           still applies to the raw level before the ratio is taken.
//
//     DESC  a plain-English description, shown when you hover the
//           event's name in the table. Two sentences: what the release
//           measures, and why traders watch it. May be empty for an
//           event that has no figure to explain - a market holiday
//           says everything it knows in its name.
//
//           It is LAST in the row on purpose. It is the only
//           free-text field and by far the longest, so putting it at
//           the end keeps every fixed field at a stable offset and
//           makes a row readable by eye up to the point it starts.
//           It can contain no '|' and no newline; both are rejected
//           at build time, because either would add a phantom field
//           and Pine SKIPS any row whose field count is wrong -
//           silently, leaving the event as UNKNOWN KEY.
//
// OCCURRENCE RECORD - exactly 10 chars, no delimiters:
//
//     DDHHMMKKKI
//     | |   |  +-- impact  1 char   0=holiday 1=low 2=med 3=high 4=critical
//     | |   +----- key     3 chars  base36 index into the key table
//     | +--------- HHMM    4 chars  UTC time, 9999 = all-day / tentative
//     +----------- DD      2 chars  UTC day of month, zero-padded
//
//     base36 alphabet: 0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ
//
// A month chunk is the bare concatenation of its records, so record i
//     is str.substring(chunk, i * 10, i * 10 + 10)
//     and the count is str.length(chunk) / 10.
//
// Records are pre-sorted ascending by DDHHMM. Pine never sorts them.
//
// WORKED EXAMPLE
//
//     02090001W2  ->  2024-09-02 09:00 UTC, key 01W = Unemployment Rate, impact 2
//
// All timestamps are UTC. Conversion to the chart's timezone happens
// at render time only.
// ===================================================================

// The packed occurrence records, one string per UTC month, in
// chronological order starting at CHUNK_BASE_YM.
//
// Deliberately an array of separate push statements rather than a
// switch: Pine limits how long one statement may be, and a 37-arm
// switch over this much literal data exceeds it (CE10205). Index
// arithmetic replaces the branch and costs less at runtime.
monthChunks() =>
    array<string> out = array.new<string>()
    array.push(out, "")  // 2024-09  151 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2024-10  156 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2024-11  149 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2024-12  143 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-01  158 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-02  141 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-03  145 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-04  155 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-05  153 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-06  152 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-07  159 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-08  146 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-09  153 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-10  157 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-11  138 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2025-12  155 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-01  153 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-02  142 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-03  150 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-04  163 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-05  151 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-06  156 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-07  162 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-08  148 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-09  157 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-10  156 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-11  155 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2026-12  156 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-01  142 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-02  144 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-03  156 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-04  154 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-05  143 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-06  158 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-07  154 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-08  145 events
    array.push(out, "")  // 2027-09  158 events
    out

// y * 12 + m of the first month held in the array above.
CHUNK_BASE_YM = 24297

// Returns the packed occurrence records for one UTC month, or an
// empty string outside the generated horizon.
//
// The array is built inside the call rather than kept in a global:
// an exported library function may not read an array from the
// library's global scope (CE10227). The indicator calls this at most
// 37 times, all on bar 0, so the rebuild is paid once.
export monthChunk(int y, int m) =>
    array<string> chunks = monthChunks()
    int idx = y * 12 + m - CHUNK_BASE_YM
    idx >= 0 and idx < array.size(chunks) ? array.get(chunks, idx) : ""

// Event metadata, one newline-separated line per canonical event.
// Field order: KKK|NAME|RGN|CAT|TVF|UNIT|DEC|POL|SCL|DRV|DESC
export keyTable() =>
    "000|Fed Interest Rate Decision|US|POL|INTR|%|2|1|1|0|The US Federal Reserve sets the interest rate that banks charge each other overnight. It is the single biggest scheduled driver of the dollar, bond yields and share prices.\n001|FOMC Press Conference|US|POL|||0|0|1|0|The Fed chair takes questions from journalists shortly after a rate decision. Markets often move more on the tone of these answers than on the decision itself.\n002|FOMC Minutes|US|POL|||0|0|1|0|A detailed account of the Fed meeting held three weeks earlier, naming the arguments made on both sides. Traders read it for hints about the next decision.\n003|Fed Balance Sheet|US|POL|CBBS|T|2|0|1000000000000|0|The total value of bonds and other assets the Fed holds. A shrinking balance sheet drains money from the financial system, which tends to tighten conditions.\n004|Inflation Rate YoY|US|INF|IRYY|%|1|1|1|0|How much consumer prices have risen over the past twelve months. Inflation is what the Fed is trying to control, so this print moves rate expectations more than almost any other.\n005|Inflation Rate MoM|US|INF|IRMM|%|1|1|1|0|How much consumer prices rose in a single month. It is noisier than the annual figure but shows a turn in the trend sooner.\n006|Core Inflation Rate YoY|US|INF|CIR|%|1|1|1|0|Annual inflation with food and energy stripped out, because those two swing wildly for reasons monetary policy cannot touch. The Fed watches this more closely than the headline.\n007|Consumer Price Index|US|INF|CPI|idx|2|1|1|0|The raw price index that the inflation rates are calculated from, rather than a percentage. Published for completeness; the rate figures are what traders react to.\n008|Producer Price Inflation MoM|US|INF|PPIMM|%|1|1|1|0|How much the prices factories and farms receive for their goods changed in a month.           "K|0|-1|1000|0|How many people filed for unemployment benefits for the first time last week. Being weekly, it is the fastest read there is on whether the job market is turning.\n00J|Continuing Jobless Claims|US|LAB|CJC|K|0|-1|1000|0|How many people are still claiming unemployment benefits after their first week.
